_verificationNote.whyNotIndexed: IRC 225 (added by P.L. 119-21 sec. 70202) contains no inflation-adjustment clause. Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (the 2026 inflation adjustments) has NO section for IRC 225, confirming the $12,500/$25,000 caps and the $150,000/$300,000 thresholds are the same fixed statutory figures for tax years 2025 through 2028.
_verificationNote.sunset: No deduction for any taxable year beginning after 2028-12-31 (IRC 225(g)). This file must not be cloned forward past tax year 2028.
howToRecheckAnnually: 1. Schedule 1-A (Form 1040), Part III — the authoritative computation, including the rounding convention: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040s1a.pdf
2. IRS FAQ fact sheet on the qualified overtime deduction (currently FS-2026-13, Aug 2026): https://www.irs.gov/pub/taxpros/fs-2026-13.pdf
3. IRS Notice 2025-69 — definition of the FLSA overtime premium: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-25-69.pdf
4. The year's IRS inflation-adjustment revenue procedure — check whether an IRC 225 section has appeared: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf
_verificationNote.roundingIsDeliberatelyDifferent: phaseOut.fractionCountsAsFullStep is FALSE here, and that is correct. Schedule 1-A line 19: 'Divide line 18 by $1,000. If the resulting number isn't a whole number, DECREASE the result to the next LOWER whole number. (For example, decrease 1.5 to 1, and decrease 0.05 to 0.)' IRC 225(b)(2)(A) says 'for each $1,000' with NO 'or portion thereof'. This is the OPPOSITE of car-loan.2026.json, where IRC 163(h)(4)(C)(ii)(I) does say 'or portion thereof' and Schedule 1-A line 28 rounds UP. The three flags must never be 'harmonised'.
_verificationNote.fixedOn: 2026-08-15 — fractionCountsAsFullStep flipped true → false, and the false branch of phase-out.ts changed from roundHalfUpToCent to Math.floor. Both changes were required: half-up rounding is not floor.
_verificationNote.scopeNote: premiumShareOfRegularRateBps=5000 is correct ONLY for FLSA-required time-and-a-half. Per Notice 2025-69, pay above the FLSA-required premium (e.g. contractual double time) is NOT qualified overtime, and overtime owed only under state law or a CBA to an FLSA-exempt employee is NOT qualified at all.
